title: Hanukkah: counting up (Shabbat 21b)
hookLine: Shammai said start with eight and go down; Hillel said start with one and go up, and Jews follow Hillel

lines: ONE CANDLE, THEN TWO, THEN EIGHT.
cards: The first night, one candle, plus the helper. The second night, two. By the eighth, the whole row is blazing and the kids are counting out loud.
The order looks obvious. In the Talmud's telling, it wasn't. Two schools of Jewish law looked at those same eight nights and disagreed.
One said start full and go down. The other said start small and go up. Both gave reasons.

teach.h: THE HOUSE OF SHAMMAI: EIGHT, THEN DOWN.
teach.b: The two schools were the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel, the students of two well-known teachers who lived around the time of Herod. They disagreed on many questions, and this is one.
The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, page twenty-one, lays it out. The House of Shammai said: on the first night, light eight, and each night, one fewer.

teach.h: THE HOUSE OF HILLEL: ONE, THEN UP.
teach.b: The House of Hillel said: on the first night, light one, and each night, one more. Then come the reasons.
Shammai's side said the lights should match the days still to come: eight days left, eight lights; one day left, one light. There's real sense in that. It's honest about time running out.
Hillel's side gave a different kind of reason: in matters of holiness, we go up, and we don't go down.
The Hebrew phrase is short, ma'alin ba-kodesh, we raise in holiness.
And Jewish practice follows the House of Hillel, as the Talmud rules it generally should.

Elsewhere the Talmud says why Hillel's school usually won: they were kind and humble, and they taught their opponents' views, even quoting Shammai's opinion before their own. Look at what that does to the eight nights.
Shammai's way is a countdown; it ends small. Hillel's way is a count up; it ends with the most light. The argument is about candles, and also about which way a practice should move.

how: Following the House of Hillel, Jews light one Hanukkah light on the first night and add one each night until eight, lighting the newest first with the shamash.

o: eight nights of lights that count down to one
dedication, with lights that count up each night
a holiday of eight lights all lit at once

games.q: you're a student in the House of Hillel. how do you say to light the Hanukkah lights?
o: eight the first night, one fewer each night.
one the first night, one more each night.
games.why: one, then up: in holiness we go up, and we don't go down. the House of Shammai counted down, but practice follows Hillel.

practice: Pick one tiny good thing to start with: a glass of water, a kind word, a page read, a minute of quiet.
Not a countdown of things to give up, but a count up of things to add, so notice the empty space beside today's one thing, where tomorrow's will go.

wordCard.voice: Hanukkah. Dedication, and a count that rises: one light the first night, eight by the last, because in holiness we go up.

orig.note: Hebrew: we raise in holiness; the House of Hillel's reason for counting up.

carryVoice: Your line: always go up. In holiness, the count only rises. See you on day one hundred thirty-two.
